newsitem.title: CHINA: Brokers concerned at Shanghai stock market drift.
newsitem.headline: Brokers concerned at Shanghai stock market drift.

text.p: The Shanghai stock exchange is under pressure from brokers to seize back the initiative to ensure it does not languish in third place behind Hong Kong and Shenzhen, analysts said on Monday.

Six months ago, Shanghai was unquestionably the premier stock market of China, but during the past few months Shenzhen has overtaken Shanghai in turnover of domestic A share trading and capitalisation of foreign currency B shares.
On Monday, turnover on Shenzhen's A share market was 4.52 billion yuan ($545 million) against 2.7 billion yuan on Shanghai's A share market.

"There's been a bit of a reordering and now we have Hong Kong at number one, Shenzhen number two and Shanghai bringing up the rear at number three," said John Crossman, Shanghai representative of Jardine Fleming.
"There's a lot of pressure from local brokers to do something about it," he said.
The pressure from brokers is to encourage the leadership of the Shanghai exchange to be more aggressive and to do more to attract good companies to list on its board.

"The Shanghai local government leadership has been passive so far this year in promoting the stock market," said a Chinese broker. "As a result, Shenzhen has taken over from Shanghai in both B-share and A-share trading turnover."
"The exchange is facing pressure from brokerages in Shanghai because it's affecting their trading," said a Hong Kong analyst.
"It would be dangerous for the Shanghai authorities to be complacent. Shenzhen will not wait. They are very ambitious and aggressive in attracting capital flows from Shanghai," the analyst said.
A spokesman for the Shanghai stock exchange declined to comment on the issue.
The brokers called on the exchange to be more active in attracting strong companies to list, to lower trading fees and to use the city government to help drum up business.
"One simple thing they can do is to go out and market for new listings," said a foreign broker in Shanghai. "At the moment, they're just waiting to companies to come to them."
But another broker said Shanghai's lack of activity was more the result of pressure from Beijing on the stock exchange, headed by Yang Xianghai, to be cautious.

"You have a man in charge of the Shanghai stock exchange who understands fairly clearly what the central government and city government leadership wish to see happen," said Richard Graham, head of ING Barings in Shanghai. "I don't think he has much option but to be cautious."

The analysts said Shenzhen would not be able to consolidate its lead over Shanghai in the longer term, given its proximity to Hong Kong and the clear signals from Beijing that it views Shanghai as the domestic financial capital.

"From a five-year perspective, Hong Kong will retain its premier position because it has the legal structure, but Shanghai will improve its competitive position against Shenzhen and I think Shenzhen will be left behind," said Jardine Fleming's Crossman.
"They're having a strong run now, but I think they've only succeeded because Shanghai has been sitting back. When Shanghai gets over it, I think it will move forward."
